source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

stimulus.text:
Section 2 of the Pendleton Civil Service Act (January 16, 1883) required the new Civil Service Commission’s rules to provide “for open, competitive examinations for testing the fitness of applicants for the public service now classified or to be classified hereunder.” The Act followed the 1881 assassination of President James A. Garfield by a disappointed office seeker.

Federal employees covered by the merit system:

| Year | Share of federal employees in the classified service |
| 1883 | about 10% |
| 1897 | about 40% |
stimulus.source_note: Pendleton Civil Service Act, Section 2, January 16, 1883 (National Archives transcript; the quoted clause is exact). Garfield’s assassination by a disappointed office seeker: 5 Steps to a 5, 2024, Chapter 18, “Gilded Age Politics,” and Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 8. Coverage shares: National Archives (about 10 percent of 132,000 employees in 1883) and the historical literature summarized in the Pendleton Act history (about 40 percent by 1897).

stem: Why did Congress pass the Pendleton Act when it did?

options.text: Voters had demanded an end to all federal jobs at once
options.misconception: The Act reformed hiring; it never proposed ending federal jobs.

options.text: The Supreme Court had ordered Congress to act
options.misconception: No court order appears. The push followed Garfield’s assassination.

options.text: Business leaders asked for more political appointments
options.misconception: Business wanted influence, but the Act cut patronage, so it did not serve that ask.

options.text: Garfield’s assassination by a disappointed office seeker showed the spoils system’s danger

rationales.A: The Act kept federal jobs and filled them by examination, so it did not end them.
rationales.B: The passage names the assassination, not a court order, as what came before the Act.
rationales.C: The Act took jobs out of political control, the opposite of more appointments.
rationales.D: The Act followed the 1881 assassination by a disappointed office seeker.
rationales.general:
Link the event to the law.
1. The stimulus says the Act followed Garfield’s assassination.
2. The assassin was a disappointed office seeker.
3. A murder over a government job showed the whole spoils system was dangerous.
4. Congress answered with open competitive examinations instead of patronage appointments.
Remember: a shocking event can turn a long debate into a law within two years.
